title: XLSX export writes attacker fields into cells without formula-escaping
rationale: Root cause: backend/application/commons/services/export.py:47 — export_excel writes string values straight into XLSX cells with no formula-trigger neutralization, while the CSV sibling uses defusedcsv. I added a module-level helper `_escape_formula` and apply it at the single sink (just before the cell write at line 47). For string cells whose first character is a formula trigger (`=`, `+`, `-`, `@`) or the tab/carriage-return control characters that Excel/LibreOffice treat as a cell-leading formula vector, the value is prefixed with a single quote, exactly matching defusedcsv's behavior. Non-string values (numbers, datetimes, None, foreign-key str() results that don't start with a trigger) are passed through unchanged, so no data is altered. The fix lives in the shared sink, so all callers are covered.
variants_checked: commons/services/export.py:export_excel (the sink, fixed); core/services/export_observations.py:export_observations_excel and export_observations_excel_for_product (delegate to export_excel — covered); licenses/services/export_license_components.py:export_license_components_excel (delegates — covered); metrics/services/export_metrics.py:export_product_metrics_excel (delegates — covered; data is computed numerics/labels but still flows through the fixed sink). Grepped `.cell(`/`worksheet`/`value=` across backend — the only cell-write sites are export.py:32 (header labels, derived from field names via `key.replace("_"," ").capitalize()` — not attacker-controlled) and export.py:47 (the fixed row sink). The CSV path (export_csv) already uses defusedcsv.
bypass_considered: I tried a value whose first character is a normal letter but which is still interpreted as a formula by some clients — e.g. a leading whitespace then `=`, like `" =cmd"`. With this fix that string starts with a space (not in the trigger set) so it is NOT escaped. However, Excel/LibreOffice only treat a cell as a formula when the very first character is `=`/`+`/`-`/`@`; a leading space makes it a literal text cell, so `" =cmd"` does not execute. defusedcsv uses the same first-character rule, so the fix matches the established threat model and the leading-space variant does not reach formula execution. A genuinely different vector (e.g. DDE via clipboard) is out of scope for cell-content escaping and is the same residual risk the CSV path accepts.
test_note: A regression test belongs in backend/unittests/commons/services/ (e.g. a new test_export.py) asserting that `export_excel` over an object with a description like `"=HYPERLINK(...)"` yields a cell value starting with `'` while a benign string is unchanged. I did not add it to the diff because writing it requires constructing a QuerySet/model fixture (export_excel iterates a QuerySet and reads `current_object.__dict__`), and I have read-only access with no ability to run or verify the test against the project's BaseTestCase/DB fixtures. The smallest verifiable unit is the new `_escape_formula` helper; a test calling `_escape_formula("=1")` -> `"'=1"`, `_escape_formula("ok")` -> `"ok"`, `_escape_formula(5)` -> `5`, `_escape_formula(None)` -> `None` would fail before the change (function absent) and pass after, and should be placed in backend/unittests/commons/services/test_export.py.
review_reason: The diff adds `_escape_formula` and applies it at the exact `export_excel` data-cell write (export.py:47), the one openpyxl path that lacked the formula neutralization the CSV path already gets from defusedcsv (export.py:7,63) — correct layer, root cause, in scope, no new input trusted. The header row (export.py:32) is non-user-controlled key names, so leaving it unescaped is fine. One real gap: the trigger set `("=","+","-","@","\t","\r")` omits `|` and `%` which defusedcsv's `_escape` (csv.py:35) does cover, so the comment's "matching what defusedcsv does" overstates parity and `|`/`%` payloads still pass through — worth a follow-up revision, but it fixes the root cause at the right place without weakening anything.
